content: Amoxicillin, administered as a 7-day course, is typically the first-line antibiotic for treatment. In cases where resistance to amoxicillin is reported, alternative antibiotics such as azithromycin (3-day course) or rifampicin (4-day course) are used. For Group B Streptococcus (GBS), it is recommended in many countries to identify mothers whose babies are at risk of developing GBS disease. Universal screening for GBS carriage during pregnancy is one method to achieve this. Mothers identified as being at risk are offered intravenous penicillin during labor to protect their newborns from GBS infection. Meningitis is the most recognized disease caused by invasive bacteria, with other clinical manifestations including septicaemia, pneumonia, and septic arthritis. Diagnosis is often based on microbiological tests, but cultures may not always be feasible due to factors such as lack of expertise, inadequate infrastructure, organism fragility, or early initiation of antibiotic therapy. Consequently, molecular and nucleotide sequence-based diagnostic methods are increasingly preferred. Many cases of meningitis, septicaemia, and pneumonia, as well as associated deaths, are preventable through vaccination. Effective vaccines are available for three of the four primary causative organisms: Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Vaccines for Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS) are in various stages of development. Neisseria meningitidis is classified into 12 serogroups, with A, B, C, W, X, and Y causing most meningitis cases. Streptococcus pneumoniae has at least 97 serotypes, with predominant disease-causing serotypes varying by region. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) is the most common cause of meningitis due to this organism, though occasional cases are caused by type a. Of the 10 serotypes of Streptococcus agalactiae, Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, and V are the most prevalent in causing disease. Humans are the primary reservoir for all four pathogens. Transmission occurs person-to-person via direct contact or respiratory droplets for N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae. For S. agalactiae, transmission occurs from mother to child around birth, through contact, or via nosocomial routes. The incubation period for N. meningitidis is 2–10 days, commonly 3–4 days. For S. pneumoniae, it is 1–3 days; for H. influenzae, 2–4 days; and for S. agalactiae, 1–7 days for early-onset disease and 7 days to several months for late-onset disease, typically around 3–4 weeks. The period of communicability varies: for N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae, it lasts until the organisms are no longer present in nasal or throat discharges. For H. influenzae, it can persist as long as the organisms are present in body discharges, even without nasal discharge. For S. agalactiae, the period is unknown but may extend throughout colonization or disease duration. Infants can remain colonized for several months after birth and following treatment for systemic infections. Carrier states are common for all four pathogens, with colonization sites including the pharynx for N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, and H. influenzae, and the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts for S. agalactiae. The diseases caused by these pathogens include meningitis and sepsis for N. meningitidis; pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis for S. pneumoniae; meningitis, pneumonia, sepsis, and epiglottitis for H. influenzae; and sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis for S. agalactiae. Case fatality ratios vary significantly by country and access to care, ranging from 5–20% for N. meningitidis, 20–90% for S. pneumoniae in children aged 1–59 months, 7–30% for H. influenzae in children aged 1–59 months, and 5–20% for S. agalactiae in neonates aged 0–89 days. The epidemic potential of these pathogens also varies, with N. meningitidis having a high potential, S. pneumoniae moderate, H. influenzae low, and S. agalactiae very low. Several vaccines are available against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and N. meningitidis. Vaccines for S. agalactiae (GBS) are under development, with challenges including demonstrating effectiveness and navigating regulatory pathways for licensure and WHO prequalification. Recent regulatory interactions suggest a potential pathway for initial licensure based on correlates of protection and post-licensure effectiveness studies. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) such as Pfizer’s Prevnar 13, GSK’s Synflorix, and Serum Institute of India’s Pneumosil are highly immunogenic and effective against vaccine-type invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD), pneumonia, and nasopharyngeal colonization. The choice of vaccine should consider programmatic characteristics, vaccine supply, price, local serotype prevalence, and antimicrobial resistance patterns. PCV13 may offer additional benefits in settings with significant disease attributable to serotypes 19A or 6C. The global Invasive Bacterial Vaccine-Preventable Disease (IB-VPD) Surveillance Network, coordinated by WHO since 2009, standardizes monitoring of the global burden and etiology of IB-VPDs, supports PCV introduction, and monitors their impact, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The network includes sentinel hospitals reporting cases of children under 5 years hospitalized for suspected meningitis, with laboratories conducting confirmatory tests and strain characterization using PCR. As of 2019, the network comprised 123 laboratories globally, following standardized testing and reporting protocols.
